messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: kronecker products
parts:
On 4/25/13 1:03 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, April 24, 2013 7:27:39 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
>
> The distribution indeed requires the Kronecker product, so I've followed Ben's suggestion and programmed it element
> by element. It's not fast, but will have to do for the time being ;) Thank you for taking a look!
>
>
> Glad it is somewhat functional. In a case like a multivariate normal, you might be able to speed it up a little bit by
> being clever with the products. So, if you need (in R notation)
>
> |
> t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y
> |
>
> you end up repeatedly post-multiplying Lambda by segments of y and scaling those by elements of D - a * W. Particularly
> if D - a * W is sparse, you could squeeze out some efficiency gains by using temporaries.
>
> This is one reason why Stan would need a really good implementation of Kronecker products to realize performance
> improvements, as opposed to merely having a convenient syntax for using the Kronecker product in Eigen.

We're still working on the refactor. After that happens,
we'll be in much better shape to add new data types.

We'll have the same problem (though not as extreme)
right now if we try to implement Cholesky factors.
Specifically, we'd need to get the triangular views in
the right places. One way to do that in the current setup
(that is, without changing the way the code's generated
very much) would be to have functions that were defined
specifically on triangular views like some of our functions
do now. It's clunky and we wouldn't want to replicate
all of our matrix functions for triangular views, but it
might let us squeeze out most of the performance we want.

It looks like there's an unsupported module in Eigen for
Kronecker products, but I was expecting an expression template,
not a dense product:

https://bitbucket.org/eigen/eigen/src/0cf501b7d3dd/unsupported/Eigen/src/KroneckerProduct/KroneckerTensorProduct.h

Am I reading that correctly? Line 51 looks like a killer:

AB.block(i*Br,j*Bc,Br,Bc) = A(i,j)*B;

This we could do in Stan with a function

kronecker_multiply(A,B)

and we could make the auto-diff much more efficient, but it's
still going to be a space hog.

What do people do with kronecker products once they create them?
Can we attack the problem one level up? Is one of the terms
here going to be a kronecker product?

> t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y

That's the kind of op we could wrap up.

- Bob

On 4/25/13 1:03 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, April 24, 2013 7:27:39 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:

>
>
> Glad it is somewhat functional. In a case like a multivariate normal, you might be able to speed it up a little bit by
> being clever with the products. So, if you need (in R notation)
>
> |
> t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y
> |
>
> you end up repeatedly post-multiplying Lambda by segments of y and scaling those by elements of D - a * W. Particularly
> if D - a * W is sparse, you could squeeze out some efficiency gains by using temporaries.
>
> This is one reason why Stan would need a really good implementation of Kronecker products to realize performance
> improvements, as opposed to merely having a convenient syntax for using the Kronecker product in Eigen.

We're still working on the refactor.  After that happens,
we'll be in much better shape to add new data types.

We'll have the same problem (though not as extreme)
right now if we try to implement Cholesky factors.
Specifically, we'd need to get the triangular views in
the right places.  One way to do that in the current setup
(that is, without changing the way the code's generated
very much) would be to have functions that were defined
specifically on triangular views like some of our functions
do now.  It's clunky and we wouldn't want to replicate
all of our matrix functions for triangular views, but it
might let us squeeze out most of the performance we want.

That is an issue but as long as the operations are not utilizing the upper triangular elements, then the waste is just allocating unnecessary zeros, which is small compared to the amount of waste involved in multiplying the Cholesky factors together and then Cholesky factorizing the product.

It looks like there's an unsupported module in Eigen for
Kronecker products, but I was expecting an expression template,
not a dense product:

https://bitbucket.org/eigen/eigen/src/0cf501b7d3dd/unsupported/Eigen/src/KroneckerProduct/KroneckerTensorProduct.h

Am I reading that correctly?  Line 51 looks like a killer:

AB.block(i*Br,j*Bc,Br,Bc) = A(i,j)*B;
My understanding is that the Kronecker module in the unsupported/ part of Eigen would be inefficient for a variety of reasons in Stan.

This we could do in Stan with a function

     kronecker_multiply(A,B)

and we could make the auto-diff much more efficient, but it's
still going to be a space hog.

What do people do with kronecker products once they create them?

In statistical applications, the A and B are usually covariance matrices (and so is the result), and then used in multivariate densities and whatnot. The result is often sparse (even if represented as a dense Eigen::Matrix<>) and often multiplied from the left and the right by the same matrix. Also, they are often used in conjunction with the vec() operator, which is easy but not implemented in Stan yet.

I started to mock up a class for this a few months ago whose unwritten methods could specialize the algebra of Kronecker products

template<typename T_A, typename T_B>
class Kronecker {
// see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_product
    typedef typename boost::math::tools::promote_args<T_covar,T_other>::type OutType;

public:
  const Kronecker(const Matrix<T_A,Dynamic,Dynamic> &,
                  const Matrix<T_B,Dynamic,Dynamic> &);
  const Kronecker(const Matrix<T_A,Dynamic,Dynamic> &);
  const Matrix<OutType,Dynamic,Dynamic> get_AoxB();
  const Matrix<OutType,Dynamic,Dynamic> get_A();
  const Matrix<OutType,Dynamic,Dynamic> get_B();
  const Kronecker transpose();
  const Kronecker inverse();
  // specialize det(AoxB), eigenvalues(AoxB), singular_values(AoxB), and trace(AoxB)
  const size_t rows() const;
  const size_t cols() const;
  const Kronecker operator* (const Kronecker &, const Kronecker &);
  const Kronecker operator* (const double, const Kronecker &);
  const Kronecker operator* (const Kronecker &, const double);
  const Kronecker operator* (const var, const Kronecker &);
  const Kronecker operator* (const Kronecker &, const var);
  const EigenBase<Derived> operator* (const Kronecker &, const EigenBase<Derived> &);
  const EigenBase<Derived> operator* (const EigenBase<Derived> &, const Kronecker &);
  const EigenBase<Derived> operator/ (const EigenBase<Derived> &, const Kronecker &);
protected:
  EigenBase<Derived> m_A;
  EigenBase<Derived> m_B;
};

Can we attack the problem one level up?  Is one of the terms
here going to be a kronecker product?

 > t(y) %*% ( (D - a * W) %x% Lambda ) %*% y

That's the kind of op we could wrap up.

Yes, the quadratic form is one thing that could be optimized but there are a lot of things.

Ben

It's not the allocation of zeroes I'm worried about.
We can even use copies of the same stan::agrad::var
instance for that. It's that if you then multiply them
without triangular views, you do a ton of extra work in
both the multiplication and in auto-dif of constant zeroes
(which our code won't be clever enough to figure out are
constant zeroes we don't care about). But then putting back
in triangular views would take care of that issue.

I was thinking we either have special triangular-view functions,
or we somehow instrument the generated code so that every use
of a cholesky factor type is automatically wrapped in a triangular
view.

Right! This is what you'd need to do for the efficient
expression template implementation in Eigen itself. As is,
they're just giving you shorthand for a big matri that
gets allocated and filled.

Maybe it makes sense writing that and contributing it
to Eigen. Not that it'd immediately help us in Stan.

The only other thing you'd need is operator()(int,int) and
operator()(int) [or whatever the right type is for indices].
